def.title: Curvature: how fast a direction turns
def.mini: Walk a curve: over a short stretch Δs your heading turns by Δθ. κ = dθ/ds. A line: κ = 0. A circle: κ = 1/R everywhere. On a surface, two directions: K = κ₁κ₂, 0 on a plane, 1/R² on a sphere.
def.text: Over a short stretch Δs of a curve the direction of the tangent changes by Δθ; the curvature is their ratio in the limit, κ = dθ/ds, in radians per metre [1]. It uses a position, a distance and an angle, nothing else. A straight line never turns: κ = 0. On a circle of radius R, an arc Δs turns the radius, and the tangent with it, by Δs/R: κ = 1/R at every point. Any other curve has, at each point, a circle that hugs it best, the osculating circle of radius 1/κ [2]. On a surface each direction has its curvature; the largest and smallest, κ₁ and κ₂, are at right angles [3], and Gauss's curvature is their product [4]: 0 × 0 on a plane, 1/R × 1/R on a sphere. On the Earth, κ = {{kEarth}} /km: one degree every {{turnDeg}} km.
def.verdict: Curvature is defined without any globe: a plane is the surface whose K is 0 at every point.
surf.title: Gauss's curvature: plane 0, cylinder 0, sphere 1/R²
surf.mini: At each point a surface bends most and least in two directions at right angles, κ₁ and κ₂. K = κ₁κ₂: 0 for a plane and for a cylinder, 1/R² for a sphere, negative for a saddle.
surf.text: Cut a surface with planes through its normal: each cut is a curve, and as the cut turns its curvature runs between a largest and a smallest value, κ₁ and κ₂, in two directions at right angles [1]. Their product K is Gauss's curvature. A plane gives 0 × 0, a cylinder 1/R × 0, a sphere 1/R × 1/R and a saddle opposite signs. Gauss proved that K, unlike κ₁ or κ₂ alone, can be measured from inside the surface with lengths and angles, and that bending without stretching never changes it [2]: a sheet rolled into a cylinder keeps K = 0, a sphere can never be flattened onto a sheet without stretching. On the Earth, K = {{KEarth}} /km².
surf.verdict: A flat Earth has K = 0 everywhere; any measured K that is not zero, from inside, is curvature.
inside.title: Curvature from inside: a triangle's angles, a circle's length
inside.mini: On a plane a triangle's angles make 180° and a circle of radius r is 2πr long. On a sphere the angles exceed 180° by A/R², and the circle is 2πR sin(r/R), shorter.
inside.text: Two ways to measure curvature without leaving the surface. Draw a triangle with shortest paths and add its angles: 180° on a plane, 180° plus K times the area on a surface of curvature K, A/R² on a sphere [1] [2]; on the Earth one second of arc of excess takes {{excPerArcsec}} km². Or walk a circle at a fixed distance r from a post, measured on the ground: on a plane it is 2πr long, on a sphere 2πR sin(r/R), shorter by about πr³/(3R²), and the shortfall gives K [3]; a circle of 100 km on the Earth is {{circ100}} m short. Only angles and lengths read on the ground enter.
inside.verdict: Would vindicate a plane: triangle sums that stay at 180°, and circles exactly 2πr long, at every size.
dip.title: The dip of the horizon, run on a plane and on a sphere
dip.mini: Simulated: {{dipN}} dips read to 1′ from 50 m to 12 km. On a sphere they line up and give {{dipSphR}} km. On a plane one reading gives {{dipPl1}} km, then the slope falls below zero: no radius.
dip.text: Simulated readings, the same places and the same 1′ errors on both surfaces. On a sphere the line of sight to the horizon is tangent to the ground and dips by δ, with cos δ = R/(R + h), so δ grows as √(2h). On a plane the far ground never goes below eye level and the dip read is the instrument's error alone. Put through the same calculation, a line through zero of δ against √(2h): the sphere's {{dipN}} readings give {{dipSphR}} km ({{dipSphLo}}–{{dipSphHi}}), correlation {{dipSphRr}}. The plane's first reading alone gives {{dipPl1}} km and any two correlate perfectly, but all of them together give a slope below zero, correlation {{dipPlRr}}: no radius. No air in this simulation.
dip.verdict: Would vindicate a plane: real dips that stay at zero, within the instrument's error, from a beach to an airliner.
zen.title: Reciprocal zenith angles, run on a plane and on a sphere
zen.mini: Simulated: {{zenithN}} lines of 10 to 120 km, each zenith angle read to 10″. On a sphere the sum exceeds 180° by d/R: {{zenithSphR}} km. On a plane the sum is 180°: no radius, at any count.
zen.text: Simulated readings, the same lines and the same 10″ errors on both surfaces. Two stations d apart read the angle from straight up to each other. With parallel verticals the two angles make exactly 180°; with verticals that meet at a centre the sum exceeds 180° by d/R. A line through zero of the excess against d gives, for the sphere's {{zenithN}} readings, {{zenithSphR}} km, correlation {{zenithSphRr}}. The plane's first reading falls below 180°, a negative radius, and all its readings together give a slope compatible with zero, correlation {{zenithPlRr}}. With air (k = {{k}}) the plane's sum would fall below 180°, by {{planeAir100}}′ at 100 km, and the sphere's excess shrink to d(1 − k)/R.
zen.verdict: Would vindicate a plane: pairs of zenith angles summing to 180°, or less with refraction, whatever the length of the line.
tri.title: Triangle angle sums, run on a plane and on a sphere
tri.mini: Simulated: {{triangleN}} triangles of 50 to 15,000 km², angles read to 0.7″. The sphere's excess grows with the area: {{triangleSphR}} km. The plane's first two give {{trianglePl1}} and {{trianglePl2}} km; all of them, no slope.
tri.text: Simulated readings, the same triangles and the same 0.7″ errors on both surfaces. On a plane the three angles of a triangle make 180°; on a sphere they exceed it by A/R² [1] [2]. A line through zero of the excess against the area gives, for the sphere's {{triangleN}} triangles, {{triangleSphR}} km, correlation {{triangleSphRr}}. The plane's first triangle, slightly above 180° by chance, gives {{trianglePl1}} km and its second {{trianglePl2}} km: two readings that do not contradict each other. With all of them the plane's slope is compatible with zero, its range runs to infinity ({{trianglePlR}} km … ∞) and the correlation is {{trianglePlRr}}.
tri.verdict: Would vindicate a plane: real triangles whose excess does not grow with their area.
circ.title: A circle walked round a post, on a plane and on a sphere
circ.mini: Simulated: {{circleN}} circles of 20 to 300 km, lengths to one part in 100,000. On a sphere C falls short of 2πr by πr³/3R²: {{circleSphR}} km. On a plane, no shortfall: no radius.
circ.text: Simulated readings, the same circles and the same errors on both surfaces, lengths only. Walk a circle at a fixed distance r from a post, measured on the ground, and measure its circumference C to one part in 100,000. On a plane C = 2πr; on a sphere C = 2πR sin(r/R), short by about πr³/(3R²) [1]. A line through zero of the shortfall against πr³/3 gives, for the sphere's {{circleN}} circles, {{circleSphR}} km, correlation {{circleSphRr}}. The plane's first circle comes out longer than 2πr, as on a saddle, and all its circles together give a slope compatible with zero, correlation {{circlePlRr}}: no radius.
circ.verdict: Would vindicate a plane: circles exactly 2πr long, within the error of the tape, at every size.
erat.title: Eratosthenes' shadows, with the flat model's nearby Sun
erat.mini: Simulated: {{eratN}} pairs of sticks. A flat Sun {{sunH}} km up gives two plausible first radii, {{eratPl1}} and {{eratPl2}} km; further from it, up to {{eratFar}} km. The sphere: one line, {{eratSphR}} km.
erat.text: Simulated readings, the same places and the same 0.1° errors on both surfaces. Two sticks d apart on the line towards the point under the Sun; the angles of their shadows differ by Δz. On a sphere with parallel sunlight Δz = d/R. On a plane with a Sun at infinity Δz = 0; flat-earth models put it about {{sunH}} km up [1], and then Δz = arctan(r₂/H) − arctan(r₁/H). Near the point under that Sun the plane gives a radius close to H, {{eratPl1}} and {{eratPl2}} km for its first two pairs; at 8,000 km it gives {{eratFar}} km. All the plane's pairs together scatter around their best line by χ²/ν = {{eratPlChi}}, against 1 for the instrument's error; the sphere's {{eratN}} lie on one line, {{eratSphR}} km, χ²/ν = {{eratSphChi}}. Two shadows are not a test; many are.
erat.verdict: Would vindicate the flat Sun: shadow pairs that give a radius growing with their distance from the point under the Sun, as (H² + r²)/H.
travel.title: Speed × time over angle, run on a flat-earth map and on a sphere
travel.mini: Simulated: {{travelN}} trips of known speed. On a sphere v t = Rθ: {{travelSphR}} km. On the flat-earth map the first trip gives {{travelPl1}} km, but southern trips give {{travPlSouth}} km: no single radius.
travel.text: Simulated readings, the same trips and the same errors (1.5 % plus 20 km) on both surfaces. A seismic wave or an airliner of known speed v goes between two places in a time t; the angle θ between them comes from their latitudes and longitudes with the sphere's formula, and R = v t / θ. On a sphere v t = Rθ, and the {{travelN}} trips give {{travelSphR}} km, χ²/ν = {{travelSphChi}}. On a plane laid out as the flat-earth map centred on the North Pole (a degree of latitude worth πR/180 km), v t is the straight distance on the map: its first trip gives {{travelPl1}} km, plausible, but the map stretches east–west trips, more in the south: {{travPlSouth}} km for southern trips against {{travPlNorth}} km for northern ones, χ²/ν = {{travelPlChi}}. Using the sphere's formula for θ does not make a plane fit a sphere.
travel.verdict: Would vindicate the plane: travel times at known speeds that fit straight distances on one flat map, in the south as in the north.
fail.title: Two ways a radius calculation fails on a plane
fail.mini: Simulated, same instrument on both surfaces. Triangles on a plane: r falls to {{trianglePlRr}}, χ²/ν stays at {{trianglePlChi}}, no curvature. Eratosthenes under a nearby Sun: r stays at {{eratPlRr}}, χ²/ν climbs to {{eratPlChi}}. Sphere: r = 1, χ²/ν ≈ 1.
fail.text: Two checks on a fitted line, followed reading by reading on simulated surveys. The correlation r says whether the readings follow a line at all; χ²/ν compares their scatter around it with the instrument's known error, about 1 when the line holds. On a plane the radius calculation fails in one of two ways. Triangle angle sums carry only the instrument's error: the correlation falls to {{trianglePlRr}} while χ²/ν stays at {{trianglePlChi}}, readings perfectly consistent with no curvature at all. Eratosthenes' shadows under a flat-model Sun 5,000 km up carry a signal of their own, so the correlation stays at {{eratPlRr}}, but no single radius fits them: χ²/ν climbs to {{eratPlChi}}. On the sphere, with the same instrument, r stays at 1 and χ²/ν near 1 in both. One or two readings never show which: two readings always correlate perfectly. The figures show the 300 simulated triangles of both surfaces with their lines through zero, then r and χ²/ν against the number of readings.
fail.verdict: Would vindicate a plane: real readings whose correlation with distance or area stays near zero, or whose radius changes with where they are taken.
